I believe governments should legally recognize same-sex marriage nationwide.

My reasoning rests on several foundations. First, there's a straightforward equality principle: if marriage is a legal institution with real consequences—tax benefits, hospital visitation rights, inheritance protections—denying it based on sexual orientation treats some citizens as lesser. I don't see a compelling government interest that justifies this differential treatment.

Second, religious objections to same-sex relationships, however sincere, shouldn't determine civil law in pluralistic societies. Legal marriage is distinct from religious marriage. Protecting religious institutions' autonomy to define marriage according to their beliefs (which most proposals do) adequately respects conscience while maintaining equal civil rights.

Third, empirical concerns—that marriage equality harms children, families, or religious freedom—haven't materialized in countries and regions that've adopted it. Same-sex couples benefit from legal recognition the same way different-sex couples do.

I recognize this involves genuine value tensions. Some people hold deep convictions about marriage's meaning. But when those convictions conflict with others' fundamental interests in equal treatment and family security, I think equality should prevail, especially when religious practice remains protected.

The practical case is also strong: legal recognition provides concrete protections to real people and families who currently lack them. That concrete benefit outweighs abstract concerns about traditional definitions.
